Porsche launches entry-level 911 Challenge racer

By
Daniel Lloyd
-
Aug 26, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 3:34
Instaread

Porsche has launched a new entry-level customer racecar based on the 911 GT3 that will be eligible for its Sprint Challenge one-make series.

The Porsche 911 Challenge shares plenty of parts with its road-going counterpart, with Porsche describing it as ‘near-production’.

It is designed to race in the Porsche Sprint Challenge, a one-make competition platform comprised of various regional series including one in the UK which supports the British Touring Car Championship. The GB series will adopt the car from 2027.

In Sprint Challenge, the 911 will replace the Cayman 718 GT4 Clubsport which has also been used as Porsche’s GT4-class contender for several years.

The Challenge is the fourth new 911 racing model that Porsche has launched in the last year or so.

The German manufacturer this year introduced a new Cup Car to the top rung of its one-make pyramid and followed that up with a new GT4 contender to replace the Cayman in 2027.

Advertisement

These moves unite all of Porsche’s GT racing activities under the 911 platform, which is topped by the 992.2-generation 911 GT3 R for the global GT3 category.

Production parts

As an entry-level platform, the 911 Challenge features more production parts than the other racing 911s.

Key carry-over items include the seven-speed dual-clutch PDK gearbox, the steering wheel which has been lifted from a GT3 RS and updated, and air conditioning.

Targeted at owners and drivers looking to make their first steps in motorsport, the car has plenty of support functions including ABS, traction control, ESC (electronic stability control) and torque vectoring as part of a variable driving dynamics system.

The 911 Challenge is powered by a water cooled, 4.0-litre six-cylinder boxer engine which Porsche says is ‘largely derived’ from the production 911 GT3.

Its power output has been marginally increased to 508bhp at 8500rpm – it revs up to 9000rpm.

‘Since their introduction, the GT3 models have shaped Porsche’s identity as a sports car manufacturer like almost no other model range,’ said Thomas Laudenbach, vice president of Porsche Motorsport.

‘They are conceived and developed in close collaboration with motorsport.

‘The 911 Challenge, this tradition is being expanded to include a model that allows new customer groups to experience the thrill of motorsport in a 911.’

Some areas of the car have undergone greater levels of modification, such as the dampers which has been tuned for the rigours of racing.

The rest of the suspension system (double wishbone front, multi-link rear) consists of forged control arms with top mounts and a three-way adjustable anti-roll bar.

The 911 Challenge runs with slick tyres on 18-inch wheels secured with five-stud mounting, as seen on the new 911 GT4.

Another carry-over item from the GT4 is the set of 380mm x 32mm steel brake discs, working in conjunction with four-piston aluminium monobloc racing calipers.

Although the bodywork has been transplanted from the 911 GT3 onto the 911 Challenge, the interior has been stripped out and fitted with the usual motorsport features including a welded-in rollcage, bucket seat and six-point harness.

‘The 911 Challenge brings the driving experience of the road-legal 911 GT3 into customer motorsport more directly than ever before,’ said Porsche Motorsport head of sales Michael Dreiser.

‘Drivers can get to grips with it without a long learning curve and can complete their first kilometres on the racetrack in a familiar vehicle design.

‘We are following a principle here that dates back to the 1960s: our customers receive a race-ready car complete with motorsport safety technology, data acquisition, spare parts support and technical documentation.’
